title: Phala Confidential AI Compromised
story_key: story|title:phala confidential ai compromised
content_excerpt: We are publishing preliminary findings from a security incident affecting Phala infrastructure. Two groups of users may need to take action: We contained the incident on November 8. The affected model service has been restored with additional protections and monitoring. The attacker made further attempts after our KMS root key rotation on November 6, and we have observed no successful unauthorized access since containment. Our investigation and comprehensive verification of the remediation remain in progress. We are limiting exploit-specific details until this work is complete. We will then publish a full root cause analysis (RCA). We are sorry this happened, and we appreciate the patience of everyone checking their systems and rotating credentials. On November 5, we detected unauthorized activity on one server. The attacker chained a legacy internet-facing service with management interfaces that relied on loopback access for trust and did not independently authenticate callers. This allowed the attacker to create unauthorized CVMs and obtain application credentials. We blocked the identified access paths that day. On November 6, we rotated the KMS root key used to derive application secrets. On November 8 UTC, a third-party security researcher provided evidence that request data sent to DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 had been exposed. We traced this evidence to an inference deployment on a new GPU server. It was serving production traffic without our full production security hardening. The attacker used a similar access pattern to take control of the inference VM, making in-flight request data visible during processing. We took the deployment and its model offline. The attack sequences and associated infrastructure overlap. Our current assessment is that a single actor conducted both intrusions, and we are treating them as one incident. All times are UTC. This is a condensed operational timeline, not an exhaustive forensic log. In-flight request contents may have been exposed for requests sent to Phala's deployment of this model during the window above. Treat any credentials or other sensitive information in those requests as compromised. From July 1 through November 7, the researcher regularly included unique, per-request canary credentials in requests to Phala and monitored them for subsequent use. title: Article: LLM Reliability Layers Under Test: Accuracy, Yield, and the Limits of Verification
summary:
Verification layers sort outputs by trust rather than fixing errors. In a benchmark of six reliability layers, voting and self-correction failed to recover accuracy - they only withheld doubtful records. Production systems gain more reliability by replacing generation with deterministic lookups, tracking yield over raw accuracy, and resolving extraction bottlenecks before stacking checks.

By Pushpdeep Mishra, Wejdan Bagais

title: Encoder Disaggregation in vLLM: Scaling Multimodal Serving with EPD
summary: Recent advances in vLLM encoder disaggregation: metadata-only multimodal requests, dedicated encoder execution, remote embedding transfer, cross-encoder caching, and lower-overhead EPD routing.
story_key: model:vllm|title:encoder disaggregation in vllm scaling multimodal serving with epd
content_excerpt: Multimodal inference adds an encoding stage before language-model execution. Images, video frames, and audio must be processed into embeddings before the language model can use them. The demand on this stage varies with media size, modality, and request mix, and can change independently of prefill and decode demand. Encoder / Prefill / Decode (EPD) disaggregation separates these stages into independently deployed vLLM instances. Recent work in the vLLM community has expanded EPD across model execution, remote embedding transfer, shared caching, multimodal input handling, and request routing. DeepSeek's inference deployment Q&A describes an E/P/D architecture with a separately deployed vision encoder. vLLM has supported encoder disaggregation since our December 2025 architecture post , and continues to improve that support. vLLM main now also supports metadata-only EPD for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. This post explains the engineering behind that progress, with a focus on five changes: The EPD tracker links the ongoing work. The core vLLM capabilities described below, including MiMo and XPU support, are included in vLLM v0.32.0. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash metadata-only support is available on main through #62802 . The vLLM Router and SMG integrations below use their respective main branches. EPD supports two deployment patterns: E+PD , with a separate encoder and a combined prefill/decode instance, and E/P/D , with all three stages deployed separately. Figure 1. E+PD separates encoding from language-model execution. E/P/D additionally separates prefill and decode. EC connectors deliver encoder embeddings; KV connectors transfer the state between prefill and decode. An image-heavy workload may need more encoder capacity without a corresponding increase in decode capacity. A workload with longer responses may require the opposite. Separating the stages allows operators to adjust their instance counts and execution settings independently, while moving encoder computation off the GPUs serving the language model. Transferring embeddings solves only part of the handoff. The consumer also needs enough information to reconstruct the multimodal input layout: placeholder lengths, image grids, feature lengths, and identifiers linking those positions to the transferred embeddings. A straightforward EPD implementation sends the original media to the encoder, transfers the resulting embeddings through an EC connector, and forwards the original request to P/PD. title: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents
summary: Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings requires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across complex, multi-tool workflows. We present a three-phase comparative study of three evaluation frameworks, each representing a distinct evaluation paradigm (trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics), applied to two analytics agents in a controlled research setting using frozen execution traces. Phase 1 quantifies evaluation harness stability through repeated measurements, finding that 97% of configurations meet the stability threshold and that stability patterns are agent-independent. Phase 2 measures known risk detection on 72 ground-truth test cases, where the trace-based framework achieves the best precision-recall balance (F1=0.90) while text-only evaluation matches on recall but generates 5x more false alarms. Phase 3 evaluates unknown risk discovery, uncovering 24 novel failures with zero overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming. Our results demonstrate that (1) the information available to the evaluation harness determines evaluation quality, (2) functional and security evaluation are complementary, and (3) LLM-based evaluation harnesses surface subtle errors that human reviewers miss. We recommend a two-framework strategy: trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial red-teaming for security validation.

title: FERN: Cross-Benchmark Table Retrieval for Text-to-SQL with Frozen Retrievers and Learned Ranking
summary: Text-to-SQL systems over large pooled catalogs must first retrieve the tables a question needs. We compare against the published table recall of RASL, which uses Claude 3.5 models to extract keywords and select tables, on pooled BIRD, Spider, and Fiben catalogs. FERN (Feature-Engineered Ranking with No generative LLM) instead fuses three frozen retrievers into 100 candidates, describes each with up to 120 features, and reorders them with LightGBM rankers fitted once on BIRD's training questions. On Spider, where it was not fitted, its candidate pool alone reaches RASL's published recall at fifteen tables (98.0), and the ranker raises the share of questions with every gold table in the top five (complete@5) from 83.9% to 95.6%. At five tables, FERN's recall is within one point of RASL's on Spider (96.7 vs 97.0) and on BIRD with its evidence hints (96.6 vs 97.5), and 8.2 points below on BIRD without them (89.3). On 121 real BEAVER questions, without BEAVER fitting, its recall at fifteen (82.1) falls between two BEAVER-trained retrievers (80.8, 84.5), but its complete@15 is below both (49.6 vs 54.5 and 62.0). On Fiben, it falls far short at fifteen tables (54.2 vs 69.2, different question sets), although its recall at fifty is numerically close to RASL's question-only retrieval result (80.7 vs 79.4). On BIRD dev with evidence, non-retrieval features raise complete@5 by 7.7 points over retrieval signals alone. On BIRD dev, median latency is 208 ms per question on one A100, without hosted model calls.

title: Can KV Cache Be Reused Across Model Updates? A DeepSeek-V4-Flash Case Study
summary: Reusing key--value (KV) caches across language model updates could avoid repeated computation of shared context, but changes in model weights raise a fundamental question about what these caches preserve. We investigate direct cache reuse across four model updates, with a detailed study of DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Flash-0731. Our central finding is that caches can retain useful task information without faithfully reproducing the updated model's behavior. Retrieval accuracy varies substantially across updates, ranging from near-native performance to large losses. With source caches already available, reuse achieves median time-to-first-token speedups of $2.10$--$5.08\times$ on three longer-prefix QA benchmarks. To characterize the behavioral differences behind these outcomes, we introduce Functional Cache Divergence, which compares next-token distributions under reused and native caches. Direct KV cache reuse better preserves native model behavior in natural-text continuation, whereas compatibility degrades with increasing prefix length in single-token retrieval tasks. Answer-margin analyses help explain how correct retrieval decisions survive substantial internal state changes. Yet even agreement on the first generated token does not ensure agreement in answer content or stopping behavior. These findings establish task utility and fidelity to native inference as distinct criteria for evaluating cross-version KV cache reuse.

title: GitHub affordances as human-agent conveyances
story_key: story|title:github affordances as human agent conveyances
content_excerpt: Thinking about how GitHub PRs and issues are becoming the primary surface for collaboration between humans and agents. I've been noticing the growing use of GitHub, or rather core GitHub building blocks, as the natural choice for work management between humans and agents. Specifically issues and pull requests. One example close to me and my colleagues is how my friend and boss Tom Jung manages the identification, parcelling and specification of tasks for his agents to work on, as issues in the repo for our tutorial system . Another example is how that work is then managed in the form of pull requests (PRs), which I guess is a natural consequence of the first observation. Incidentally, this makes me think that this also changes the issue mechanism as a conveyance for work items rather than mere problem statements. A net positive, perhaps. Anyway, it's on the topic of PRs that I came across two blog posts from folks I have admired for a long time. In Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary> , Simon Willison uses HTML's details disclosure element to avoid the TL;DR reaction "I'm not reading all of that" to super-detailed agent-written descriptions which, while not incorrect, are too deep for the purposes of overview by a human. In “Doctor, it hurts when agents create unreviewable PRs.” “Don’t do that.” , Jon Udell describes the problem of agents raising PRs with thousands of lines that that are nigh on impossible to properly understand. He maintains (and I agree) that the PR should be a shared context between humans and agents, and - while some would say that using agents to review such monsters would be one solution to that 1 - smaller chunks of work are the answer. Both approaches allow the PR to remain the unit of work for tracking and review, and make room for the human to still be the active arbiter in the decision process. In traditional terms, the PR can stay primarily a letter, rather than a ledger. With many others, both Simon and Jon are exploring the paths ahead with existing tools and mechanisms, coming up with approaches that are pragmatic workarounds which eventually become norms. Something that the online community has been doing for decades.

title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge
summary: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution, which is based on $π_{0.5}$. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392. Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks (semantic stages built from the demonstrations' skill annotations, task and stage embeddings of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls); variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching with a simple noise-vs-compute model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations; and a 200k-step training run, about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstrations. A cloud evaluation infrastructure keeps a shared record with provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators on one GPU together faster than real time. On top of the learned policy, 14 tasks are routed to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent that controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. Across these 14 tasks, Astra's mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy. The public submission included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.

title: Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class: A Policed Quality-of-Service Mechanism for Agentic AI Traffic, Evaluated from Simulation to Real-Kernel Adversarial Testing
summary: Software agents built on large language models generate traffic unlike human web traffic, yet routers have no class for it and cannot verify a sender's claim to be an agent. This paper proposes the Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class (VATC), which combines a reserved Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) value declaring agent traffic, a router-side classifier that demotes flows contradicting the declaration to a class served after best-effort traffic, and a rate-limited priority queue. VATC was compared with static Differentiated Services (DiffServ), a dedicated class that trusts the marking, and fq_codel, a per-flow fair-queuing scheduler, in two simulators and on a real Linux kernel. VATC matched DiffServ under steady load. In a constructed burst it cut mean agent queuing delay by 98% relative to DiffServ in simulation (assuming an immediate verdict), at a 12% increase in human delay; most of the gain came from the separate class. Under a spoofed flood in the kernel, the rate limit held human latency 11 times below DiffServ's. Without verification, DiffServ and a tightly configured fq_codel gave legitimate agents lower latency than VATC; a live four-feature classifier then demoted all 20 bulk-shaped spoofers and gave agents 0.30 ms, but missed six spoofers that copied the agent pattern. With emulated network delay, a timing feature of the classifier stopped separating agent from human flows. In real agent harnesses on a congested link, router queueing took 13% to 63% of task time, depending on harness and assumed model latency. The traffic was synthetic or sandbox-scale.

title: Guy Podjarny: Building a Software Factory You Can Trust
summary:
Software development is moving from building the car to building the factory, but concerns about quality, cost and safety hold many teams back. In this opening keynote, Guy Podjarny, Founder & CEO of Tessl, lays out a path to a software factory you can trust: skills that define what good looks like, self-improving loops that learn from what they observe, and factories built around business outcomes. He shares real data from Tessl's own factory, from automated vulnerability remediation to cutting cost per PR. Recorded at AI DevCon New York 2026.

What we cover:
– Why quality, cost and safety concerns hold back software factories
– Delegating to agents like a good manager: skills to loops to factory
– Automated vulnerability remediation with skills
– Verifiers that set limits on an agent's empowerment
– Self-improving loops, and cutting cost per PR from $75 to $13
– From shared skills to a factory per product

Author matches published credits. Year applies to posts; wiki entries have no author or publication year. You can also use author:"Ada" or type:podcast in non-regex searches. November 9, 2026 — Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 arrive on Anthropic’s IPO roadshow day. How much thinking is worth paying for? On Friday, we asked Jamin Ball what comes next for Anthropic’s IPO . On Monday the roadshow started and Anthropic shipped the long-anticipated next-version of Claude Fable and Mythos . Of course, it is the new top model in the world, taking back Opus 5.5’s #1 spot from Gemini 4 Carbon which had its brief moment in the sun (10 days). Fable comes with a 20% per token price cut… but is more token hungry, as both SemiAnalysis GDPx and Artificial Analysis agree: Fable 5.1 cost $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. Fable 5.2 costs $8 and $40 . Yet on GDPx, a benchmark of professional tasks, SemiAnalysis paid $88.15 per task, up from $67.16 . The run logs give a clue. Where Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 would try about 20 test cases, 5.2 sometimes wrote hundreds or thousands and spun up subagents to check its work independently. All that checking helped Fable take first place at 16.4% . You pay for the checks either way. Which effort setting should you put in production? On FrontierCode 2.0, Anthropic reports that Fable at High matched Opus 5.5 at Max for about half the cost per task… but don’t talk about Fable at Max. AI News for 11/07/2026-11/09/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! Top Story: Claude Fable 5.2 / Mythos 5.2 Benchmarks, Economics, Restrictions, and First Impressions Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, claiming both are "a step above Opus 5.5 in almost all the capabilities we evaluated." It tops most independent leaderboards. It also arrives with deliberate RSI nerfs, heavier per-task costs and restricted subscription access. Launch claims. @claudeai announced the pair as built for "the most daunting technical challenges," with gains in coding, reasoning and vision. @marktenenholtz flagged unusual system-card phrasing: "The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2

title: How We Optimized Browser Use for Deep Agents
summary: We compared seven browser toolsets for Deep Agents, picked Stagehand from Browserbase, and tuned it with LangSmith traces and evals. Here's what we learned.
story_key: story|title:how we optimized browser use for deep agents
content_excerpt: Browser agents can now take on multi-step work that's painful and time-consuming for people. Personal agents like Instinct and Meta's Muse plan cross-country road trips, cancel unused subscriptions, and list cars for sale, all on sites with no public APIs. DataDome saw agentic browser requests jump 4.7x in September alone. Browser use helps in two places: actions an API can't cover, like using a website the agent wasn't set up for, and end-to-end testing of the web apps coding agents build. Either way, the agent needs two things: This post focuses on the tools, and on making them good enough that the agent uses the browser well. We set out to give agents in Managed Deep Agents a browser. We compared seven toolsets and picked the best one, Stagehand ( GitHub ) from Browserbase . Then we improved it based on what agents did in LangSmith traces, and validated every change with evals. The biggest lesson was how much room there is to improve an agent through tool design. Browser use toolsets come in a few forms: native tools, an MCP server , or a CLI the agent runs in a shell. Browser use poses two unique challenges for those tools: We iterated with the agent development lifecycle : run the agent on a benchmark, read its traces in LangSmith to see where it wasted steps or tokens, change the tool, and run evals to check that the change helped. Every run was a LangSmith experiment , so we could compare setups side by side and click from any number into the trace behind it. We had every harness return structured output (a JSON answer). That way a formatting slip, like a one-line reply to a task that asks for a table, didn't count against its browsing. We upstreamed that option to Browserbase's evals. We first held the model and tasks fixed and changed only the toolset. The seven toolsets differ in how the agent calls them: Every toolset passed between 78% and 90% of tasks, but cost and speed varied widely. The Stagehand tools passed the most (90%) for $1.98 in total, at a median 17.4 s per task. Playwright MCP passed 78% for $26.71, about 13x the cost, and took three times as long per task ( full results ). The gap held on harder tasks. On HardBench's 38 core tasks, Deep Agents passed 30 with Stagehand's code-writing run tool and 21 with Browserbase's command-style browse CLI, at three times the cost per task. Early browser tooling repurposed testing SDKs like Playwright . As Browserbase puts it, "Playwright was built for testing, we built Stagehand for your agent

title: claude-code v2.1.321
summary:
What's changed

  • Added Claude Fable 5.2 (claude-fable-5-2), now the default Fable model — 1M context, $8/$40 per Mtok with $0.20/Mtok cache reads
  • Added --settings <file> to claude remote-control, which applies a settings file to every session it starts; if the file changes, no new session starts until you restart claude remote-control
  • Fixed MCP OAuth requests sending secrets such as refresh tokens to another host when a server redirected them
  • Fixed a case where a read-only Bash command ran outside the sandbox without a permission prompt
  • Fixed a case where Bash permission checks judged a file write from the wrong folder and didn't prompt
  • Fixed deny rules and protected-file prompts not applying to the file that a cp or mv into a directory writes
  • Fixed the "Draws from usage credits" note showing after a switch to Fable on Enterprise seats whose plan includes Fable
  • Fixed the fallback model sometimes declining a request or mentioning a stopped response when the first model was blocked before replying
  • Fixed claude mcp login printing a SEP-2352 issuer warning each time you sign in again to a server that Claude Code registered with
  • Fixed NotebookEdit deleting or overwriting a notebook's first cell when the call named no cell, on network paths (UNC shares, WSL folders, /net mounts)
  • Fixed Edit changing the first of several matches, replacing a whole file on an empty old_string, or editing a notebook as text, on network paths (UNC shares, WSL folders, /net mounts)
  • Fixed /config showing Manual as the default permission mode when new sessions start in auto mode; pressing Space on "Auto (default)" now saves Don't Ask, not Plan
  • Windows: Fixed FileChanged hooks stopping for paths set through watchPaths after the first shell command, when the session's working directory had a lowercase drive letter
  • Fixed --plugin-dir . and --plugin-dir ./builtin writing generated type files for Claude Code's built-in plugins into a builtin folder
  • Fixed context usage estimates overcounting tool definitions when exact token counts are unavailable
  • Fixed /compact showing twice in Remote Control on web and mobile
  • Fixed plugin auto-updates and /plugin marketplace updates downloading a plugin again for each worktree or folder of a repository
  • Fixed auto mode losing a background subagent's report that had started a turn when the conversation was compacted before Claude answered it
  • Fixed project skills, commands and agents staying missing after their folder was removed and came back mid-session, such as with git stash, including after entering a worktree
  • Fixed claude -p sometimes telling Claude that background commands get 30 minutes when they are stopped after 10
  • Fixed pkill, pgrep and pidwait in cloud sessions matching the session's own parent processes
  • Fixed Claude in Chrome and computer use server processes staying alive after their parent exits behind a proxy that stalls connections
  • Fixed a large hook output pointing Claude to a file that held another hook's output from the same tool call
  • Fixed apps that embed Claude Code getting their own PreToolUse hook's ask reason instead of another hook's when both asked
  • Fixed a PreToolUse hook's ask being lost when another hook's defer finished first and could not be honored
  • Fixed a rare crash on permission prompts and background tasks
  • Fixed project skills, commands and agents disappearing from the menu in SDK and desktop sessions after Claude entered a worktree
  • Fixed /desktop on macOS saying Claude Desktop is not installed when it is in ~/Applications
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry repository attributes (vcs.*) missing from Claude Desktop sessions that start on a pre-started process
  • Fixed WebFetch passing "No response from model" to Claude as page content when the model reading the page returned no text; the call now fails with a clear error
  • Fixed screen reader mode delaying the prompt at startup when the system clock moved back while Claude Code was starting
  • Fixed a command's panel sometimes not coming back after a dialog closed, leaving no panel or prompt on screen until the next redraw
  • Fixed a project's MCP server being disconnected after the first message in a Claude Desktop Code tab session when the desktop app has an MCP server or extension of the same name
  • Fixed a turn ending with "API Error: EPROTO: The TLS handshake failed" when the connection broke partway through a reply; the partial reply is kept or the request is retried, as before 2.1.302
  • Fixed high memory use in long sessions that repeatedly read single lines from large files
  • Fixed fast mode losing replies, switching models or retrying for minutes when fast serving is rate-limited, overloaded or failing; it now tries standard speed on the same model first
  • Fixed one request carrying far more background agent reports than intended after Claude was stopped while several were waiting
  • Fixed messages from a Claude Desktop Code tab session to your other sessions staying paused after you typed while Claude was still working
  • Fixed claude agents ignoring --permission-mode, --dangerously-skip-permissions, --model, --effort or --agent typed before agents when a flag such as --verbose was also on the line
  • Fixed a case where Remote Control showed as off with "login expired" in the desktop app while its connection was still up, because the app was briefly unable to hand over a sign-in token
  • Fixed a Remote Control message sent with "Queue for later" reaching Claude in the middle of the running turn
  • Fixed the git status given to Claude at session start reading as clean when git status failed; it now reads as unavailable
  • Fixed the git status given to Claude at session start showing the first listed file as staged when its changes were not staged
  • Fixed a hang or out-of-memory crash when a connector in a cloud session lists resources with very long names
  • Fixed Remote Control showing as connected after its connection closed for good while the session's history was still uploading
  • Fixed screen reader mode turning off when you return to a conversation from agent view
  • Fixed screen reader mode y/n questions taking as yes a stray "y" at the end of text typed as the question opened
  • Fixed cloud sessions telling Claude that a host is probably not allowed when it is allowed and the network proxy could not connect to it
  • Fixed an MCP server sometimes showing as connected with no tools after it was reconnected or the session's directory changed while its tools were still loading
  • Fixed Bash commands sometimes running in the wrong folder when Claude sent several at once and an earlier one changed folders
  • Fixed files Claude sends from cloud and Remote Control sessions failing at once when an upload gets an HTTP 507 from a proxy; the upload now gets a second try
  • Fixed new messages not being saved, and claude -p, SDK and VS Code sessions hanging, when memory ran out while the transcript was being read
  • Fixed sign-in, token refresh and logout waiting indefinitely when something on the network accepts the connection but never answers the TLS handshake
  • Fixed a sent file showing under a different name in the Claude apps when its name hid text-direction or control characters; Claude now refuses to send such a file
  • Fixed sub-agent progress summaries running a request to its end after the model replied with a tool call
  • Fixed Bash reads such as grep -r foo "$PWD/src" asking for permission when the same command with the path typed out runs without asking
  • Fixed Claude apps gateway refusing to start when a desktop setting holds a field newer than the gateway, such as a managed MCP server's oauth.omitResource; it now warns and serves it
  • Fixed Bash commands coming back empty for zsh users whose .zshrc sets KSH_OPTION_PRINT
  • macOS: Fixed "Unable to read managed policy settings" at startup when a valid MDM profile was slow to read: the read is retried once, and a timeout is now reported as a timeout
  • Fixed agent view erasing another agent view's saved input text when it restarted for an update with nothing typed
  • Fixed remote sessions giving no reply after a restart when a UserPromptSubmit hook blocked a replayed permission answer; these hooks no longer run on that replay
  • Fixed claude remote-control accepting a y typed without Enter at its first-run question when the terminal's input ended
  • Fixed Claude Desktop not showing spend limit warnings behind a Claude apps gateway whose policy has no code: rules
  • Fixed fullscreen sessions with some plugins ending with an error when a tool result that had got shorter scrolled off the top of the screen
  • Fixed prompt suggestions making extra API requests when the model replied with a tool call
  • Fixed PreToolUse mcp_tool hooks on stdio and HTTP MCP servers being skipped when their answer was over 16 MiB; the tool call is now refused
  • Fixed skill and command names holding a Bamum letter that some fonts draw as blank: they are now refused
  • Fixed claude -p on Linux exiting 0 in silence when a full NFS export or a used-up NFS quota lost transcript lines: it now prints an error and, in text and json output, exits 1
  • Fixed background agents being reported as stopped by the user, and refused a resume, when a service interrupted a cloud session and nobody pressed Stop
  • Fixed NotebookEdit reporting success to hooks and telemetry when the edit failed, for example when the notebook changed while the permission prompt was open
  • Fixed a blank screen or no answer at startup, and empty claude mcp list output, when a stored MCP sign-in record was null
  • Fixed the Artifact tool telling Claude to add filters when an artifact's database collection is too large to sort; it now says to read the collection page by page and sort the results
  • Fixed a restarted cloud session dropping a message with a large image when the restart came before Claude's first reply to it
  • Fixed a restarted cloud session leaving a subagent's message to the main conversation unanswered
  • Fixed Claude not being told when you stop or pause a running workflow, so it no longer says the workflow is still running
  • Improved the /model picker: "More models" is now an unnumbered row below every other, and older models open under it without renumbering the rest
  • Gateway: Improved spend limits on a busy replica, which now skips fewer checks and records spend sooner
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's sign-in limit messages in Claude Code and on the /device page: they no longer name gateway settings, which the gateway's own log still names
  • Improved claude install and the install scripts: they finish 2 to 4 seconds sooner
  • Improved how soon a Remote Control session whose process crashed can pick up a new message
  • Windows: Improved startup and first-command time by finding programs on PATH without starting a helper process
  • Improved auto mode in headless sessions, the desktop app and VS Code: reports from background subagents that wait together are answered in one model call, as in the terminal
  • Improved the agent view's row for a claude --bg --worktree session that couldn't set up its worktree: it now shows the error from its beginning, not an internal tag or its last 200 characters
  • Improved the messages shown when an artifact is in another organization: /login is offered only if it's one of yours, and Claude now says where a copy may be after an account move
  • Improved sessions with more images than fit in one request: Claude is told whether it has already seen a dropped image, and repeat reads of an unchanged image are limited
  • Improved claude remote-control's messages for an unanswered first-run question: each now says what to do next
  • Improved start-up time by loading trusted TLS certificates faster
  • Improved Claude apps gateway error messages to show the gateway's address without any user name or password
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's spend limit error: the reset now shows in your local time, such as "resets 4pm (America/Los_Angeles)"
  • Windows: Improved startup time with a standard Git for Windows install by no longer checking which git.exe to run on every launch
  • Updated the session-feedback message and the allowedProviders setting description to name Ultra alongside Pro and Max, and the forceLoginMethod description to cover every paid Claude plan
  • Updated the bundled dataviz skill to suggest a list of meters, one row per item, for several ratios that each have their own limit
  • Updated the "Upgrade to Max" options to say "Upgrade to Max or Ultra"
  • Changed mods Claude writes to turn on without asking in auto and bypass modes, even with managed allowUnsandboxedCommands: false or allowManagedDomainsOnly, and not to load in dontAsk mode
  • Changed mods' own tool calls ($.tool.call, $.mcp.call) to raise no permission prompt, even under your own ask rules or in dontAsk and -p runs; deny rules and organization policy still apply
  • Changed saved Fable 5.1 model picks to move to fable: on Pro and Max plans at once, on Team and Enterprise plans once your organization allows it; use /model claude-fable-5-1 to switch back
  • Changed the fast mode labels in /fast, /config and /model to name your current model when it supports fast mode, and removed "(Opus only)" from the VS Code row
  • Changed nested skill loading: .claude/skills folders inside ~/.claude/plugins no longer load when Claude works on files there
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed an on-demand runner that the server refuses because it is not needed (session ended or paused, work order superseded) to exit 0 instead of 1
  • Windows: Changed how Claude Code finds programs it starts itself, such as git, to skip relative and UNC PATH entries and links onto a network share, and to pick up PATH changes from settings
  • Changed OpenTelemetry hook events in non-interactive sessions to leave two built-in hooks out of num_hooks and num_success after Bash and PowerShell calls
  • Changed the number of messages a Claude Desktop Code tab session can send to your other sessions before it waits for you to type again from 10 to 20
  • Changed AskUserQuestion in claude -p and SDK sessions to deny a host's permission answer that sets the undocumented afkTimeoutMs input field
  • Changed managed extraKnownMarketplaces: a declared name can't be added from another source, an entry from elsewhere is hidden, and plugins the declared marketplace lists are reinstalled from it
  • Changed Claude in Chrome tools that an app running Claude Code provides, such as the Claude desktop app's Code tab, to follow your organization's Claude in Chrome policy
  • Changed policy_mode: layered in the Claude apps gateway: managed MCP servers now add up over every matching policy, match: {} included, so a gateway already on it serves more after the upgrade
  • Gateway: Changed Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry upstreams to ignore the ANTHROPIC_*_BASE_URL variables in the gateway's environment. Set base_url on the upstream to use another endpoint
  • Changed headless sessions to reload mods in .claude/skills when their files change; set CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIR_WATCH=0 to turn this off
  • Changed the Cyber Verification Program sentence on a cyber safeguard block to use the same words as claude.ai
  • Changed Cowork cloud sessions: a PostToolUse hook can no longer replace the answer to AskUserQuestion or the plan in ExitPlanMode's result; Claude reads the originals
  • Changed cp and mv spelled by a path, such as /bin/cp, to get the same path checks as cp and mv
  • Changed background command notifications and TaskStop results to show Claude only the start and end of a command over 1,000 characters, which saves context
  • Changed artifact design guidance to treat Inter and Space Grotesk as good default typefaces
  • Changed the account email check to refuse only a shell command that holds your email and names a User-Agent, without asking, so other commands and scheduled runs no longer stop at its prompt
  • Changed Remote Control sessions to keep the folder they were started in: a connected client can no longer move a session to another folder
  • Changed managed extraKnownMarketplaces take-overs from an undeclared source: saved data is set aside for cleanupPeriodDays, and options and secrets until claude plugin restore-set-aside
  • [VSCode] Added a warning above the prompt box when both an auth token and an API key are set, matching the terminal's startup warning
  • [VSCode] Fixed a plugin's permission request showing a name with hidden characters: it now reads "a plugin"
